explain.say: Every height on a British map is measured from the average sea level at Newlyn in Cornwall, recorded by a tide gauge from 1915 to 1921. Builders need heights too: does this drain fall the right way? Surveyors find them by levelling. On the board, a strip of ground and the level line of sight from an instrument.

explain.say: Look at the flat line. A level is a telescope that turns only in a perfectly horizontal plane. First, sight a staff held on a benchmark, a point of known height, here one hundred metres. The staff reads one point two five zero. That backsight lifts us to the height of the line of sight, the height of instrument: one hundred and one point two five.

explain.say: Now swing to point A. The staff reads two point eight seven five, a foresight. Take it away from the height of instrument: point A sits at ninety eight point three seven five metres. From the same set-up, B reads two point one four five and C reads zero point six three. A big staff reading means low ground or high ground?

explain.say: Low ground, because more staff shows below the line of sight! There is a second way, rise and fall: work out how much each point rises or falls from the last. It takes more sums but checks every reading. Either way, finish with the check: the sum of backsights minus the sum of foresights equals the last level minus the first.

explain.say: Over long sights the Earth curves away and air bends the light, together about sixty seven millimetres over one kilometre. That is why surveyors keep backsight and foresight distances short and equal, so the errors cancel. Great work! faq.a: Levelling finds the heights of points relative to a datum using a level, a telescope that sights a horizontal line, and a graduated staff held on each point.

faq.q: What is the height of instrument method?
faq.a: Add the backsight to the benchmark level to get the height of the line of sight, the HI; then subtract each later staff reading from the HI to get each point's reduced level.
asks: How do you calculate reduced levels?

faq.a: A benchmark is a fixed point of known reduced level, such as a marked bolt or pillar, used to start and close a line of levels.

faq.q: What is the rise and fall method?
faq.a: Each staff reading is compared with the one before: a smaller reading is a rise, a larger one a fall. Adding rises and subtracting falls gives each level, with a full arithmetic check.
asks: Rise and fall vs HI method

faq.q: Why should backsight and foresight distances be equal?
faq.a: Equal sight lengths cancel the errors from Earth curvature, refraction and a slightly tilted line of sight, because each affects both readings equally.

facts: Ordnance Datum Newlyn is based on mean sea level measured at Newlyn, Cornwall, between 1915 and 1921.
The combined curvature and refraction correction is about 0.0673 d² metres, with d in kilometres: about 67 mm at 1 km.

quiz.say: A benchmark is at 25.000 metres. The backsight is 1.420 and the foresight on point P is 2.035. What is the reduced level of P?
quiz.show: BM = 25.000 m, backsight 1.420 m, foresight on P 2.035 m. RL of P?

wrong.1: That adds both readings to the benchmark.
wrong.2: That adds the foresight and subtracts the backsight.

quiz.say: A larger staff reading than the last one means the ground has…

quiz.why: More staff showing below the line of sight means the point is lower.
